title: Fields, factors, and the action on roots
subject: foundations
summary: Fix the ground field, separate irreducibility from separability, and translate factorization into a permutation action.
questionsAnswered: How do irreducible factors appear in a Galois group?
Why does proving irreducibility not determine the group?

sections.title: Start with the field
sections.body:
A nonconstant polynomial \(f\in K[x]\) is irreducible over a field \(K\) if a factorization \(f=gh\) in \(K[x]\) forces one factor to be constant. The field is part of the question: \(x^2-2\) is irreducible over \(\mathbb Q\), but splits over \(\mathbb Q(\sqrt2)\). Over an algebraic closure, every polynomial of degree greater than one factors. Thus absolute irreducibility is a substantive higher-degree question for polynomials in several variables, not for a single-variable polynomial.

For \(f\in\mathbb Z[x]\), first remove the content, the greatest common divisor of its coefficients. Gauss's lemma says that a primitive polynomial has a factorization of positive degrees over \(\mathbb Q\) exactly when it has one over \(\mathbb Z\). This is why congruences, divisibility, and integral coefficient bounds can answer a rational question. A constant factor such as the \(2\) in \(2x+2\) is a unit over \(\mathbb Q\), but is not a unit over \(\mathbb Z\).

citations.note: Polynomial rings, content, and irreducibility over fields and unique factorization domains.
A proof of Gauss’s lemma and its use in rational irreducibility tests.

sections.title: Keep repeated roots separate
sections.body:
Here separable means that all roots in an algebraic closure are distinct. For nonzero \(f\), this is equivalent to \(\gcd(f,f')=1\). Every irreducible polynomial over a field of characteristic zero is separable. In positive characteristic, the qualifications matter: \(x^p-t\in\mathbb F_p(t)[x]\) is irreducible, yet has only one distinct root in its splitting field.

Before using a permutation group on \(n\) roots, verify separability. Before studying an intended polynomial family, remove known factors only when the normalization is stated explicitly. The group of the original polynomial and the group acting on a selected factor need not be the same permutation representation.

citations.note: Separable polynomials, the derivative criterion, and perfect fields; numbering refers to the free version 5.10.

sections.title: The bridge: factors are orbits
sections.body:
Theorem · factor–orbit correspondence

Let \(f\in K[x]\) be separable of degree \(n\), let \(L\) be its splitting field, and let \(G=\operatorname{Gal}(L/K)\). The action of \(G\) on the roots is faithful. Its orbits are exactly the root sets of the irreducible factors of \(f\) over \(K\). In particular, \(f\) is irreducible if and only if \(G\le S_n\) is transitive.

Proof mechanism

An automorphism fixing \(K\) carries a root to another root of its minimal polynomial. Conversely, the isomorphism between the simple extensions generated by two roots of the same irreducible polynomial extends to an automorphism of the normal splitting field. These are exactly the roots in one orbit. Faithfulness follows because the roots generate \(L\).

This gives a useful order of work: determine possible factor degrees, establish transitivity, then obtain enough additional permutations or invariants to identify the group. A transitive action is a starting point, not a claim that every permutation occurs.

citations.note: Irreducibility is equivalent to transitivity for a separable polynomial.

sections.title: Worked example: one cubic, two extensions
sections.body:
Example · \(x^3-2\)

Eisenstein at \(2\) proves irreducibility over \(\mathbb Q\). Write \(\alpha=\sqrt[3]{2}\) and let \(\zeta_3\) be a primitive cube root of unity. Its splitting field is \(L=\mathbb Q(\alpha,\zeta_3)\). The real field \(\mathbb Q(\alpha)\) has degree \(3\), and adjoining the nonreal element \(\zeta_3\) has degree \(2\). Hence \([L:\mathbb Q]=6\), so the faithful subgroup of \(S_3\) is all of \(S_3\).

Over \(\mathbb Q(\zeta_3)\), the same splitting field has degree \(3\), and the group is cyclic of order \(3\). Over \(\mathbb Q(\alpha)\), the polynomial already has a linear factor and the splitting-field group has order \(2\). The polynomial expression alone does not specify its arithmetic.

citations.note: Field extensions, splitting fields, and explicit low-degree Galois theory; the displayed degree calculation is supplied here.

sections.title: Four questions that should remain distinct
sections.body:
• Factorization: is \(f\) irreducible, or what are its irreducible factor degrees?
  • Permutation group: which subgroup of \(S_n\) acts on the roots?
  • Field realization: which extension of \(K\) is the splitting field, including its ramification?
  • Uniform family statement: does the conclusion hold for every parameter, outside an explicit exceptional set, or with a limiting probability?

The word primitive also has several meanings: relatively prime integer coefficients; a permutation action with no nontrivial block system; or a finite-field element generating the multiplicative group. None of these definitions implies the others. Throughout the atlas, hypotheses belong beside the claim they support.

related.why: Reduction modulo primes converts integer factorizations into restrictions on rational factor degrees.
At good primes, the factor–orbit correspondence becomes a statement about cycle lengths.
Transitivity must be strengthened before a large symmetric or alternating group can be forced.
Absolute irreducibility in several variables survives extension of the ground field and is a different problem.

questions.title: Does irreducibility force the full symmetric group?
questions.body: No. The polynomial \(x^4+1=\Phi_8(x)\) is irreducible, but its splitting field is \(\mathbb Q(\zeta_8)\) and its group is \((\mathbb Z/8\mathbb Z)^\times\cong C_2\times C_2\), acting transitively on four roots. The modular and reciprocity entries explain two consequences of this example.

citations.note: Cyclotomic extensions and their automorphism groups.

title: Irreducibility by reduction modulo primes
subject: criteria
summary: Use one finite-field factorization, or intersect the possible degrees supplied by several primes. Understand why the method can fail for an irreducible polynomial.
questionsAnswered: When does irreducibility modulo p prove irreducibility over Q?
How can reducible reductions still prove rational irreducibility?
Can every irreducible polynomial be detected this way?

sections.title: Preserve the degree
sections.body:
Theorem · reduction criterion

Let \(f\in\mathbb Z[x]\) be primitive of degree \(n\ge2\). If a prime \(p\) does not divide its leading coefficient and \(\bar f\in\mathbb F_p[x]\) is irreducible, then \(f\) is irreducible over \(\mathbb Q\).

The leading-coefficient condition is essential. For example, \(2x^2+3x+1=(2x+1)(x+1)\) becomes the irreducible linear polynomial \(x+1\) modulo \(2\). The degree drop destroys the inference. No squarefreeness hypothesis is separately needed for the reduction criterion: an irreducible polynomial over a finite field is already separable.

Why it works

Gauss's lemma turns a putative rational factorization into \(f=gh\) in \(\mathbb Z[x]\). Since the product of the leading coefficients is not divisible by \(p\), both factors retain their positive degrees after reduction. Their reductions would factor \(\bar f\), a contradiction.

citations.note: Reduction modulo a prime and the Gauss-lemma proof.

sections.title: Keep all possible factor degrees
sections.body:
Suppose the irreducible factors of \(\bar f\), listed with multiplicity, have degrees \(d_1,\ldots,d_r\). Every rational factor degree must lie in

\[D_p=\left\{\sum_{i\in I}d_i: I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,r\}\right\}\cap\{1,\ldots,n-1\}.\]

A rational factor reduces to a product of some of these finite-field factors. Therefore \(\bigcap_{p\in P}D_p=\varnothing\), for any finite set of degree-preserving primes \(P\), proves irreducibility. In computation one can retain only degrees at most \(n/2\), because a reducible polynomial has a factor in that range.

This degree argument remains valid at a repeated reduction: multiplicities must be included. Its conclusion is weaker than a complete rational factorization, but it is exact. By contrast, reading the same factor degrees as a Frobenius cycle type requires a squarefree reduction.

citations.note: Reduction and coefficient methods for rational irreducibility; the subset-sum formulation follows directly from reduction of an integral factorization.

sections.title: Worked example: two incomplete tests make a proof
sections.body:
Example · \(f=x^4+x^3+x+2\)

\[\begin{aligned}f\bmod2&=x(x^3+x^2+1),\\ f\bmod3&=(x^2+1)(x^2+x-1).\end{aligned}\]

The cubic has no root in \(\mathbb F_2\), so it is irreducible there. The two quadratics have no roots in \(\mathbb F_3\), so they are irreducible there. Modulo \(2\), a proper rational factor could have degree \(1\) or \(3\). Modulo \(3\), it could only have degree \(2\). The sets are disjoint; hence \(f\) is irreducible over \(\mathbb Q\).

The proof certificate is the pair of displayed factorizations together with the root checks. Finding the primes may take a search; checking the resulting certificate is short and exact.

citations.note: The reduction principle underlying the certificate; these two displayed factorizations are calculated for this entry.

sections.title: An obstruction that no prime search removes
sections.body:
The polynomial \(x^4+1\) is irreducible over \(\mathbb Q\): translating by \(1\) gives \(x^4+4x^3+6x^2+4x+2\), Eisenstein at \(2\). Nevertheless it is reducible modulo every prime. At \(2\) it is \((x+1)^4\). For odd \(p\), its roots are primitive eighth roots of unity; since \(p^2\equiv1\pmod8\), they lie in \(\mathbb F_{p^2}\), so all irreducible factors have degree at most two.

In fact degree \(2\) remains compatible with every reduction, so even intersecting all the sets \(D_p\) does not prove irreducibility here. Group theory explains the obstruction: \(C_2\times C_2\), the Galois group, contains no \(4\)-cycle. For a separable irreducible polynomial over \(\mathbb Q\), Chebotarev and the Frobenius factorization theorem show that an irreducible good reduction exists exactly when the group contains an \(n\)-cycle.

citations.note: A complementary quartic example and a proof that reduction at every prime can fail.
The relation between Frobenius conjugacy classes, factorization types, and Chebotarev density.

sections.title: How to choose the next method
sections.body:
Start with cheap good primes and record possible factor degrees, not just whether the reduction is irreducible. If the intersection quickly becomes empty, save the factorizations as a certificate. If the intersection stabilizes, inspect coefficient valuations and structural symmetries. Repeated reductions may be useful for Newton polygons, while reciprocal or compositional structure can predict why particular cycle types never appear.

Failure of a finite prime search is an inconclusive computation. A proof that the group has no \(n\)-cycle is a mathematical explanation of failure of the single-prime test. These are different kinds of evidence.

citations.note: Good-prime factorizations as Galois-group information.

related.why: Gauss’s lemma is the link from rational factors to integral factors.
Valuations can extract information from primes where reduction alone has repeated factors.
Squarefree modular factorizations supply cycle types as well as factor-degree restrictions.
Exact finite-field irreducibility tests verify the modular certificate.

questions.title: Does every irreducible rational polynomial have an irreducible reduction?
questions.body: No. The precise condition is that the Galois group contain a full-length cycle. The polynomial \(x^4+1\) is a concrete counterexample to an unconditional converse.

citations.note: Chebotarev gives primes in each available conjugacy class.
An explicit failure of the converse.

title: Schönemann–Eisenstein and one-edge Newton polygons
subject: criteria
summary: A divisibility pattern can force every factor to have the full degree. Translation and Newton slopes extend the elementary criterion.
questionsAnswered: Why does divisibility by p, but not p², prove irreducibility?
What can a change of variable reveal?
How does the one-edge Dumas criterion extend Eisenstein?

sections.title: The elementary criterion and its proof
sections.body:
Theorem · Schönemann–Eisenstein

Let \(f=a_nx^n+\cdots+a_0\in\mathbb Z[x]\), with \(n\ge1\). Suppose a prime \(p\) satisfies \(p\nmid a_n\), \(p\mid a_i\) for \(0\le i\lt n\), and \(p^2\nmid a_0\). Then \(f\) is irreducible over \(\mathbb Q\).

Proof mechanism

A factorization into positive degrees can be taken in \(\mathbb Z[x]\). Reducing it modulo \(p\) gives a factorization of the monomial \(a_nx^n\). Both reduced factors are monomials of positive degree, because their leading coefficients remain nonzero. Thus both original constant terms are divisible by \(p\), which would make \(a_0\) divisible by \(p^2\).

Schönemann's work of 1846 precedes Eisenstein's 1850 paper. Cox's historical account explains their different motivations and the connection with finite fields and the division of the lemniscate. The mathematical content should be separated from the later naming convention.

citations.note: Original historical source.
Eisenstein’s original treatment.
Historical attribution and the elementary form of the criterion.

sections.title: Translate before testing
sections.body:
For \(a\in K^\times\) and \(b\in K\), substitution \(x\mapsto ax+b\) is an automorphism of \(K[x]\) and preserves irreducibility. It can change coefficient divisibility dramatically. Reversing coefficients, \(f^*(x)=x^{\deg f}f(1/x)\), also preserves irreducibility when \(f(0)\ne0\).

Example · a hidden Eisenstein polynomial

\[(x+1)^4+1=x^4+4x^3+6x^2+4x+2.\]

The right side is Eisenstein at \(2\), proving irreducibility of \(x^4+1\). More generally, if \(p\) is prime,

\[\Phi_p(x+1)=\frac{(x+1)^p-1}{x}=\sum_{j=1}^{p}\binom pj x^{j-1}\]

is Eisenstein at \(p\): all intermediate binomial coefficients are divisible by \(p\), while the constant coefficient is exactly \(p\).

citations.note: The prime cyclotomic example after translation.

sections.title: Schönemann’s residue-power form
sections.body:
The repeated reduction need not be a power of a linear polynomial. Let \(\phi\in\mathbb Z[x]\) be monic with irreducible reduction modulo \(p\), let \(e\ge2\), and let \(M\in\mathbb Z[x]\) satisfy \(\deg M\lt e\deg\phi\) and \(\gcd(\bar\phi,\bar M)=1\). Then

\[f=\phi^e+pM\]

is irreducible over \(\mathbb Q\). Indeed, a monic integral factorization would reduce to \(\bar g=\bar\phi^a\), \(\bar h=\bar\phi^b\), where \(a,b>0\) and \(a+b=e\). Write \(g=\phi^a+pg_1\), \(h=\phi^b+ph_1\). Comparing with \(f\), then dividing by \(p\) and reducing modulo \(p\), forces \(\bar\phi\mid\bar M\), a contradiction.

For example, \((x^2+x+1)^2+2=x^4+2x^3+3x^2+2x+3\) is irreducible: \(x^2+x+1\) is irreducible over \(\mathbb F_2\), and \(M=1\). This uses a higher-degree irreducible residual factor, rather than a monomial reduction.

citations.note: Historical source of the residue-power criterion.
Modern statement of Schönemann’s criterion.

sections.title: Replace valuation one by a coprime slope
sections.body:
Theorem · one-edge Dumas criterion

Let \(f=a_nx^n+\cdots+a_0\in\mathbb Q_p[x]\), with \(a_0a_n\ne0\), \(v_p(a_n)=0\), and \(v_p(a_0)=k>0\). Suppose \(\gcd(n,k)=1\) and

\[v_p(a_i)\ge k\left(1-\frac{i}{n}\right)\qquad(0\lt i\lt n),\]

where \(v_p(0)=+\infty\). Then \(f\) is irreducible over \(\mathbb Q_p\). For a rational polynomial, this also proves irreducibility over \(\mathbb Q\).

The Newton polygon has one segment of slope \(-k/n\), so every root has valuation \(k/n\). A monic factor of degree \(d\) over \(\mathbb Q_p\) would have constant coefficient of valuation \(dk/n\), an integer. Coprimality forces \(n\mid d\). Hence no proper positive factor degree is possible. Eisenstein is the case \(k=1\).

citations.note: Classical source for the Newton-polygon criterion.
Introduction states Dumas’s criterion in reversed-coefficient form; the form here follows by coefficient reversal.
Roots and slopes over a discretely valued field.

sections.title: Worked example beyond the elementary test
sections.body:
Example · \(f=x^5+4x+4\)

At \(2\), the nonzero coefficient points are \((0,2),(1,2),(5,0)\). The middle point lies above the segment joining \((0,2)\) to \((5,0)\). Its slope is \(-2/5\), and \(\gcd(2,5)=1\). Thus \(f\) is irreducible over \(\mathbb Q_2\), hence over \(\mathbb Q\).

The ordinary criterion at \(2\) does not apply to the displayed polynomial, since \(4\mid f(0)\). The Newton polygon uses the denominator of the root valuation, rather than insisting that the constant term have valuation one.

citations.note: The one-edge criterion used here; the valuation diagram and polynomial are an explicit worked computation.

sections.title: What the criterion does not decide
sections.body:
A polygon with several edges, or one whose endpoint increments have a common divisor, need not imply reducibility. It may simply leave several possible degrees. Combine primes, use residual polynomials, or change the variable. Nor does local irreducibility identify the full global Galois group.

Even allowing every integral translation does not make the elementary Eisenstein test complete. Conrad proves that \(x^4-10x^2+1\) is irreducible over \(\mathbb Q\), but \((x+c)^4-10(x+c)^2+1\) is never Eisenstein for any \(c\in\mathbb Z\). This is a useful reason to maintain several genuinely different proof methods.

The stronger one-edge criterion succeeds after translation: at \(c=1\) the polynomial becomes \(x^4+4x^3-4x^2-16x-8\). Its \(2\)-adic coefficient valuations are \(3,4,2,2,0\), and the lower polygon is a single edge of slope \(-3/4\). Dumas therefore proves irreducibility even over \(\mathbb Q_2\). The failure of every ordinary Eisenstein shift is compatible with a successful Newton-polygon proof.

citations.note: Irreducibility and failure of every integral Eisenstein shift.
The one-edge criterion applies to the translated quartic, whose coefficients and valuations are calculated here.

questions.title: Can every irreducible integer polynomial be made Eisenstein by an integral translation?
questions.body: No. The irreducible polynomial \(x^4-10x^2+1\) is a counterexample. This statement concerns integral translations; it does not classify all other changes of variable or every valuation-theoretic criterion.

title: Newton polygons, factor degrees, and large cycles
subject: criteria
summary: Read p-adic root valuations from coefficients, sharpen factor-degree restrictions with residual polynomials, and use suitable slope denominators to force a large Galois group.
questionsAnswered: What information does a Newton polygon encode?
How can several primes prove irreducibility?
What can prove irreducibility when one Newton edge still allows proper factors?
When does a local slope force containment of the alternating group?

sections.title: A geometric record of valuations
sections.body:
Write \(f(x)=\sum_{i=0}^n a_ix^i\in\mathbb Q_p[x]\) with \(a_0a_n\ne0\), and normalize \(v_p(p)=1\). The Newton polygon is the lower convex hull of the points \((i,v_p(a_i))\) with \(a_i\ne0\). Missing coefficients have infinite valuation and do not contribute finite points.

Theorem · slopes and roots

A segment of slope \(-u/v\), in lowest terms with \(v>0\), and horizontal length \(\ell\), corresponds to exactly \(\ell\) roots of valuation \(u/v\), counted with multiplicity. There is a factor over \(\mathbb Q_p\) consisting of all roots with each given valuation.

For a factor over \(\mathbb Q_p\), the number of its roots belonging to that slope must be a multiple of \(v\). Indeed, the constant coefficient of its corresponding monic slope factor has integer valuation. Thus the possible factor degrees are sums of multiples of the slope denominators, bounded by the lengths available on the respective segments.

citations.note: Definition and root–slope theorem.

sections.title: Local restrictions can contradict each other
sections.body:
A rational factor remains a factor over every \(\mathbb Q_p\). Consequently its degree must satisfy the restrictions from every prime used. This is the same logic as combining finite-field factor degrees, with finer local information. A particularly useful prime may be one for which all roots collapse to a repeated root modulo \(p\).

The polygon-product rule explains the mechanism: the segments of the product polygon are assembled from those of the factor polygons, ordered by slope. Integral lattice lengths constrain how much of a segment a factor can use. Dumas already combined such restrictions at several primes; Bonciocat develops explicit criteria using arbitrarily many primes.

citations.note: Historical source for the polygon-product and several-prime method.
Systematic several-prime irreducibility criteria.

sections.title: A residual polynomial sharpens a single edge
sections.body:
A Newton edge records valuations but forgets the leading residues of the coefficients on that edge. Retaining them can eliminate factors that the slope denominator alone permits.

Criterion · one edge with irreducible residual polynomial

Let \(f(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{ed}a_ix^i\in\mathbb Z_p[x]\) be monic. Suppose its Newton polygon is the single segment from \((0,hd)\) to \((ed,0)\), where \(h,e,d\) are positive integers and \(\gcd(h,e)=1\). Define

\[R_f(Y)=\sum_{j=0}^{d}\overline{\frac{a_{ej}}{p^{h(d-j)}}}\,Y^j\in\mathbb F_p[Y].\]

The polygon hypothesis makes every displayed quotient integral. If \(R_f\) is irreducible, then \(f\) is irreducible over \(\mathbb Q_p\).

Proof

In a monic factorization \(f=g_1g_2\) over \(\mathbb Q_p\), the factors have integral coefficients. All roots have valuation \(h/e\), so the constant coefficients show that the factor degrees are \(ed_1,ed_2\), with \(d_1+d_2=d\). The residual-polynomial product rule gives \(R_f=R_{g_1}R_{g_2}\), with degrees \(d_1,d_2\). This rule follows directly from coefficient multiplication: terms on the edge survive after normalization and reduction; terms above it vanish. If two indices summing to a multiple of \(e\) are individually not multiples of \(e\), their integral valuations put their product strictly above the edge. Irreducibility of \(R_f\) therefore forces one factor degree to be zero.

Example · a quartic certified at a repeated reduction

For \(f=x^4+2x^2+4\) at \(p=2\), the points \((0,2),(2,1),(4,0)\) lie on one edge of slope \(-1/2\). Its denominator leaves a possible quadratic factor. Here \(h=1,e=2,d=2\), and

\[R_f(Y)=1+Y+Y^2.\]

This quadratic has no root in \(\mathbb F_2\). Thus \(f\) is irreducible over \(\mathbb Q_2\), and hence over \(\mathbb Q\), although its ordinary reduction is \(x^4\). The criterion does not assume tame ramification. When \(d=1\), it recovers the one-edge Dumas criterion.

citations.note: The product rule and residual-polynomial irreducibility criterion. The elementary specialization and quartic calculation are worked out here.
The same criterion is encoded by a complete type; the source explains its ramification and residue-degree information.

sections.title: Worked example: a truncated exponential of degree six
sections.body:
Example · an exact two-prime certificate

\[F(x)=6!\sum_{j=0}^6\frac{x^j}{j!}=720+720x+360x^2+120x^3+30x^4+6x^5+x^6.\]

The coefficient valuations, from constant to leading term, are

\[\begin{array}{c|rrrrrrr}i&0&1&2&3&4&5&6\\\hline v_2(a_i)&4&4&3&3&1&1&0\\ v_3(a_i)&2&2&2&1&1&1&0\end{array}.\]

At \(2\), the vertices are \((0,4),(4,1),(6,0)\). The slopes are \(-3/4,-1/2\), with lengths \(4,2\). The only proper factor degrees permitted are \(2,4\). At \(3\), there is one segment from \((0,2)\) to \((6,0)\), with slope \(-1/3\); the only proper factor degree permitted is \(3\). Hence \(F\) is irreducible over \(\mathbb Q\).

This finite calculation illustrates the broader Newton-polygon proof for exponential Taylor polynomials. It is a proof for this polynomial, not a deduction from a numerical root plot.

citations.note: Newton-polygon treatment of exponential Taylor polynomials; the degree-six valuation table is calculated here.
The local theorem justifying the factor-degree restrictions.

sections.title: From a denominator to an alternating group
sections.body:
Criterion · a useful form of Hajir’s Newton-index theorem

Let \(f\in\mathbb Q[x]\) be irreducible of degree \(n\). Suppose a prime \(q\) divides the denominator, in lowest terms, of some Newton slope of \(f\) at a finite prime. If

\[\frac n2\lt q\le n-3,\]

then \(\operatorname{Gal}(f/\mathbb Q)\) contains \(A_n\).

The root valuation forces \(q\) to divide a ramification index in the local splitting field, and hence the order of the global group. Cauchy's theorem gives an element of order \(q\); because \(2q>n\), this element is a single \(q\)-cycle. Transitivity comes from irreducibility. A nontrivial block system would have both its block size and its number of blocks smaller than \(q\); an element of order \(q\) could act nontrivially on neither, which is impossible. Thus the action is primitive. Jordan's theorem then gives \(A_n\).

The discriminant decides between \(A_n\) and \(S_n\) only after this containment has been proved. A nonsquare discriminant alone does not imply the full symmetric group.

citations.note: Newton index divides the Galois-group order and a prime in the stated interval forces alternating-group containment.
Classical primitive-group theorem used in the final step.
Permutation-group background for primitivity and long prime cycles.

sections.title: Worked example: a complete symmetric-group certificate
sections.body:
Example · \(f=x^8+2x^5+6\) has group \(S_8\)

Eisenstein at \(2\) proves irreducibility. At \(3\), the Newton polygon has vertices \((0,1),(5,0),(8,0)\), hence slopes \(-1/5,0\) of lengths \(5,3\). The denominator forces \(5\) to divide the Galois-group order. Since \(8\lt 2\cdot5\), an element of order \(5\) is a single 5-cycle. Irreducibility supplies transitivity, and \(8/2\lt 5\le8-3\) puts us exactly in the criterion above. Thus the group contains \(A_8\).

The exact discriminant is

\[\operatorname{disc}(f)=2^{12}3^9\cdot79\cdot733.\]

It is nonsquare, so the group is \(S_8\). This calculation separates the three inputs: Eisenstein for transitivity, a Newton slope for a long prime cycle, and the discriminant for parity. The useful primes \(2,3\) have highly repeated reductions: \(x^8\) and \(x^5(x-1)^3\). Reading these multiplicities as Frobenius cycle lengths would be invalid.

citations.note: The Newton-index theorem proves alternating containment for the displayed octic. The valuations and resultant were computed exactly for this entry.
The discriminant-square criterion completes the group determination.

sections.title: What remains after drawing the polygon
sections.body:
A slope denominator is an arithmetic constraint, not automatically a cycle of that length. The prime-order argument above uses both the denominator and the interval \(n/2\lt q\le n-3\). If the relevant prime is smaller, an element of order \(q\) may be a product of several disjoint \(q\)-cycles. If irreducibility is unavailable, transitivity cannot be assumed.

Counterexample · a denominator two without a transposition

The polynomial \(x^4+4=(x^2-2x+2)(x^2+2x+2)\) has one Newton slope \(-1/2\) at \(2\). Its roots are \(1\pm i,-1\pm i\), and its splitting field is \(\mathbb Q(i)\). The only nonidentity automorphism acts as a product of two transpositions, never a single transposition. Its discriminant \(2^{14}\) is a square, consistently with this even action. Capelli's exceptional fourth-power case explains the factorization.

Irreducibility does not repair this inference. The irreducible quartic \(x^4+2x^2+4\) certified above also has slope denominator two. Its roots are \((\pm\sqrt2\pm\sqrt{-6})/2\), with independent sign choices, and its splitting field is \(\mathbb Q(\sqrt2,\sqrt{-6})\). Its Galois group is \(V_4\) in the transitive degree-four action: all three nonidentity elements are double transpositions. Its discriminant \(2^{10}3^2\) is a square.

For applications, separate three tasks: eliminate proper factor degrees; obtain a suitable local ramification divisor; calculate the discriminant square class. Laguerre and Taylor families are instructive because their coefficient formulas let these tasks be attacked systematically, but each has its own parameter restrictions.

questions.title: How can one sharpen a Newton polygon that leaves possible factor degrees?
questions.scope: Local factorization of a specified separable polynomial over a p-adic field
questions.body: Residual polynomials give the first refinement, illustrated above. If a residual factor is repeated, that stage may leave irreducibility undecided; higher Newton polygons refine the associated valuation and residue data. The Guàrdia–Montes–Nart theory gives a terminating local factorization procedure for separable polynomials. Choosing especially short certificates for a family is a further method-design question, rather than a general undecided local factorization problem.

title: Root location, coefficient dominance, and prime values
subject: criteria
summary: Use complex absolute values and integer evaluations to make any hypothetical factor impossible. These methods complement congruence and valuation arguments.
questionsAnswered: How can one large coefficient prove irreducibility?
When does a single prime value suffice?
What changes when coefficients are digits of a prime?

sections.title: Perron’s coefficient-dominance criterion
sections.body:
Theorem · Perron

Let \(f=x^n+a_{n-1}x^{n-1}+\cdots+a_0\in\mathbb Z[x]\), where \(n\ge2\) and \(a_0\ne0\). If

\[|a_{n-1}|>1+\sum_{i=0}^{n-2}|a_i|,\]

then \(f\) is irreducible over \(\mathbb Q\).

Proof mechanism

On \(|z|=1\), the term \(a_{n-1}z^{n-1}\) strictly dominates the sum of all other terms. Rouché's theorem gives exactly \(n-1\) roots inside the unit circle and one outside. If the monic polynomial factored over \(\mathbb Z\), one positive-degree monic factor would have all roots strictly inside. Its constant coefficient would be a nonzero integer whose absolute value is the product of numbers smaller than one, an impossibility.

The nonzero constant term prevents a zero root; monicity makes the constant-coefficient product argument decisive. The strict inequality controls roots on the unit circle. Variants exist, but they require their own hypotheses.

citations.note: Original source for coefficient-dominance irreducibility.
A modern presentation of Perron’s criterion.

sections.title: Worked example: reverse the polynomial
sections.body:
Example · \(x^5+3x+1\)

Reverse its coefficients:

\[f^*(x)=x^5f(1/x)=x^5+3x^4+1.\]

Now \(3>1+1\), so Perron's criterion proves \(f^*\) irreducible. Since the constant term of \(f\) is nonzero, coefficient reversal preserves factorizations and proves \(f\) irreducible. The same argument works for \(x^n+3x+1\) for every \(n\ge2\).

The method uses the location of roots, but no approximations to the roots are needed. A drawing may suggest a useful circle; the coefficient inequality supplies the proof.

citations.note: Coefficient-dominance theorem; the reversal and worked family are direct applications.

sections.title: A prime value must be sufficiently far from every root
sections.body:
Elementary prime-value criterion

Let \(f\in\mathbb Z[x]\) be nonconstant. Suppose an integer \(m\) satisfies \(|f(m)|\) prime and \(|m-\alpha|>1\) for every complex root \(\alpha\) of \(f\). Then \(f\) is irreducible over \(\mathbb Q\).

In an integral factorization \(f=gh\), each positive-degree factor has an integer leading coefficient \(b\ne0\), so

\[|g(m)|=|b|\prod_{g(\alpha)=0}|m-\alpha|>1.\]

Both factors would therefore give integer divisors of \(f(m)\) larger than one in absolute value. A practical sufficient condition is a certified root bound \(|\alpha|\le R\) and \(|m|>R+1\). This deliberately simple form is weaker than some prime-value criteria in the literature.

For example, the roots of \(x^4-10x^2+1\) are \(\pm\sqrt2\pm\sqrt3\), all of absolute value less than \(4\). At \(m=6\), the value is \(937\), a prime. Every distance is greater than \(2\), so the criterion proves irreducibility. Primality can be checked by the primes at most \(\sqrt{937}\lt 31\).

citations.note: Prime evaluations together with root or coefficient bounds; the displayed distance criterion is proved in the text.
The roots of the quartic used in the example.

sections.title: A different shortcut: the digits of a prime
sections.body:
Cohn's decimal theorem says that if \(p=a_n10^n+\cdots+a_0\) is prime, with \(n\ge1\), \(0\le a_i\le9\), and \(a_n\ne0\), then \(a_nx^n+\cdots+a_0\) is irreducible over \(\mathbb Q\). Brillhart, Filaseta, and Odlyzko extend the result to arbitrary integer bases \(b\ge2\), again assuming a nonconstant digit polynomial. The digit conditions are doing mathematical work; merely knowing one evaluation is prime is insufficient.

For instance, \(101\) is prime, so its decimal digits give the irreducible polynomial \(x^2+1\). The unrestricted prime-value inference fails for \((x-1)(x+1)\), which takes the prime value \(3\) at \(x=2\), yet is visibly reducible.

citations.note: Cohn’s theorem, prime-value root separation, and extension beyond decimal digits.
A further exposition and proof of the arbitrary-base extension.

sections.title: Where these arguments stop
sections.body:
Root location is only useful after it is connected to an arithmetic obstruction. For example, a polynomial can have all its roots real and still have a large Galois group. The special force of Perron's criterion is that a hypothetical monic factor would have an impossible constant coefficient. The special force of a suitably large prime value is that every nonconstant factor would evaluate to an integer of absolute value greater than one.

A complete factorization algorithm decides any one rational polynomial, but a uniform theorem for a sparse or parameterized family may require a new inequality or a different method. Such families provide meaningful test cases for improving these criteria.

Exact polynomial factorization algorithms.

related.why: Archimedean arguments may settle examples for which every prime reduction is reducible.

questions.title: Does one prime value prove irreducibility?
questions.scope: Integer polynomials without additional coefficient or root restrictions
questions.body: No: \((x-1)(x+1)\) takes the prime value \(3\) at \(x=2\). A distance-to-roots bound, a sufficiently large evaluation, or digit restrictions can turn a prime value into an irreducibility criterion.

title: Sparse polynomials, factor reversal, and large gaps
subject: criteria
summary: Separate persistent reciprocal factors from the nonreciprocal part, then use coefficient sparsity to constrain possible factorizations.
questionsAnswered: Why should reciprocal factors be separated in a sparse family?
What is actually proved for sufficiently large gaps?

sections.title: The family and its unavoidable obstructions
sections.body:
A useful large-gap model is

\[f_N(x)=x^N c(x^{-1})+d(x),\qquad N>\deg c+\deg d,\]

where \(c,d\in\mathbb Z[x]\) are fixed and \(c(0)d(0)\ne0\). The high and low blocks of coefficients are separated by a gap. Write \(h^*(x)=x^{\deg h}h(1/x)\). A nonconstant irreducible factor is reciprocal when \(h^*=\pm h\); the nonreciprocal part is obtained by removing all such irreducible factors, including their multiplicities.

This removal is different from removing only cyclotomic factors. Every cyclotomic polynomial is reciprocal up to sign, but a reciprocal polynomial need not be cyclotomic. A theorem about the nonreciprocal part should never be quoted as irreducibility of the original polynomial without checking the removed factors.

citations.note: Lacunary polynomial factorization and reciprocal factors.
Large-gap notation and definitions.

sections.title: A general theorem, with the structural exceptions stated
sections.body:
Call \((c,d)\) Capellian if \(-d(x)/c(x^{-1})\) is a \(p\)-th power in \(\mathbb Q(x)\) for some prime \(p\), or if \(d(x)/c(x^{-1})\) is four times a fourth power. These conditions explain systematic binomial-type factorizations.

Theorem · Schinzel, in large-gap form

Assume \(c(0)d(0)\ne0\), \(\gcd_{\mathbb Z[x]}(c^*,d)=1\), \(c\ne\pm d\), and that \((c,d)\) is not Capellian. Then there is an effective bound \(N_0\), depending on \(c,d\), such that for \(N>N_0\) the nonreciprocal part of \(f_N\) is irreducible over \(\mathbb Q\).

The cited formulation is Theorem 1.2 of Sawin–Shusterman–Stoll, attributed there to Schinzel. Filaseta–Ford–Konyagin improve explicit thresholds. Under an additional robustness condition, Sawin–Shusterman–Stoll obtain substantially more practical bounds and algorithms; that extra condition cannot be dropped when quoting their improvement.

citations.note: The general lacunary result behind this formulation.
Improved effective bounds with explicit exclusions.
Exact hypotheses of the large-gap theorem and the extra robustness assumption for its improved bound.

sections.title: The central idea: reverse one factor
sections.body:
For \(f(0)\ne0\) and a factorization \(f=gh\), form \(G=gh^*\). The reciprocal product does not change:

\[GG^*=ff^*.\]

Equivalently, as Laurent polynomials, one may use \(g(x)h(x^{-1})\); multiplication by a power of \(x\) only changes the presentation. On the unit circle, a real-coefficient polynomial satisfies \(|h^*(z)|=|h(z)|\). Consequently \(G\) and \(f\) have the same squared coefficient norm, by Parseval's identity:

\[\sum_j |[x^j]G|^2=\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}|G(e^{it})|^2\,dt=\sum_j |[x^j]f|^2.\]

For a sparse polynomial with small integral coefficients, the right side is small. There are few ways to distribute that integer norm among nonzero coefficients. Comparing the full identity \(GG^*=ff^*\) can then force the reversal to be trivial or expose a reciprocal factor. This is the mechanism behind Ljunggren's approach and its later extensions.

citations.note: Original factor-reversal approach to sparse trinomials and quadrinomials.
Small Euclidean coefficient norm as a factorization constraint.
Reversal identity and the later algorithmic development.

sections.title: Worked example: a factor recurring in one residue class
sections.body:
Example · \(x^N+x+1\)

Let \(\zeta\) be a primitive cube root of unity. Since \(\zeta+1=-\zeta^2\),

\[\zeta^N+\zeta+1=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad N\equiv2\pmod3.\]

Thus \(x^2+x+1\) divides \(x^N+x+1\) exactly in that residue class. In degree \(5\), for example,

\[x^5+x+1=(x^2+x+1)(x^3-x^2+1).\]

The cubic has no rational root, hence is irreducible over \(\mathbb Q\). This illustrates why a description of the nonreciprocal part can coexist with infinitely many reducible members of a family.

The periodicity is general for a fixed cyclotomic factor: evaluation at a root of unity depends on \(N\) modulo its order. The large-gap literature combines this elementary observation with bounds that control other factors.

citations.note: Sparse trinomial factorization and reciprocal obstructions; the displayed root-of-unity calculation is given here.
Effective eventual description by finitely many exceptional exponents and arithmetic progressions.

sections.title: A theorem for a concrete family and its boundary
sections.body:
Sawin–Shusterman–Stoll prove that \(x^N-7x^2+1\) is irreducible for every \(N\ge5\), and also for \(N=3\). The omitted degree \(4\) really is exceptional:

\[x^4-7x^2+1=(x^2-3x+1)(x^2+3x+1).\]

Their general theory supplies an eventual threshold, and a finite check handles the remaining exponents in this example. This pattern is common in family problems: a uniform argument for large parameters plus a finite exact calculation, with exceptional factors recorded explicitly.

citations.note: The complete k=7 example and its exceptional quartic.

related.why: One must distinguish the reciprocal and nonreciprocal parts before stating a sparse-family theorem.
Trinomials are the simplest setting where factor reversal and recurring cyclotomic factors are visible.
Coefficient norms and root size complement elementary dominance inequalities.
Capellian power obstructions are the binomial obstructions applied in a rational function field.
Large-gap factorization and iteration impose different parameter structures.

questions.title: How small can a uniform large-gap threshold be?
questions.scope: Pairs satisfying the hypotheses of the large-gap theorem; degree sum δ and squared coefficient weight at most w
questions.body: Sawin–Shusterman–Stoll define \(N_{\mathrm{opt}}(\delta,w)\) as the smallest uniform threshold for their Theorem 1.2 over pairs with \(\deg c+\deg d=\delta\) and \(\|c\|_2^2+\|d\|_2^2\le w\). Their Question 1.7 asks, for fixed \(\delta>1\), whether this is \(O_\delta(\log w)\); Question 1.8 asks for the uniform bound \(O(\delta\log w)\). This records the questions as posed in that paper; it is not a claim that all later work has been excluded.
